title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal and is replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis – follow live
description:
Nvidia shares fall in pre-market trading after report of Huang’s second affair

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack?

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

Continue reading...
text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal, replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis
Nvidia’s long-time boss Jensen Huang has stepped down over the scandal, and the company has appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim chief executive.
The company issued this statement just now, after its board met last night:

double quotation markThe Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately. Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

US trade representative says US 'remains concerned' about Nvidia

US trade representative Jamieson ⁠Greer ⁠said ⁠the United States “remains ⁠concerned” about the tech giant Nvidia, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI chips grapples with fallout from reports of two extramarital affairs involving its longtime ⁠chief executive Jensen Huang.
Greer told CNBC on Thursday:
double quotation markObviously we remain concerned.
Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman and former Megaspeed executive, who is accused of spying for Beijing. She has reportedly returned to China.
Wall Street to open lower with tech shares seen sliding
Wall Street is expected to have a bumpy start in just over an hour, with technology shares likely to slide again as the scandal around Nvidia boss Jensen Huang deepens.
Stock futures are extending losses, with the S&P 500 down 0.75%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 1.5% lower and Dow Jones down 0.2%.
Also, Donald Trump said: “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”
In the second half of a post about corruption in the US, on the social media platform Truth Social, he said:

double quotation markWe don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT
Oil prices have see-sawed today. Brent crude is now trading 1.5% higher at $93.98 a barrel.
Gold prices have also fallen, by about 2%.
Chinese AI companies rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity

Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China, worried that the scandal involving the US chipmaker’s chief executive Jensen Huang could lead Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors, Reuters reported.

Seeking to protect US dominance of the critical sector, Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips. But Chinese companies can access these processors remotely by renting computing power at datacentres overseas.

A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted datacentre operators about reserving it, unnamed sources told Reuters.

Meanwhile, the San Francisco-based tech publication The Information is reporting that the US Commerce Department is working to finalise a rule that will prevent Chinese artificial intelligence companies from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through datacentres located in other countries.
Alice Huang, the woman at the centre of the scandal engulfing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has returned to China and is in Beijing, according to Bloomberg News.
The chipmaker is investigating spying allegations denied by Beijing.
Nasdaq futures are now pointing to a 1% drop when the tech-heavy index starts trading later.
Megaspeed says 'committed to working constructively and transparently with US government'

Megaspeed International, the datacentre company at the centre of the scandal engulfing Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, has pledged to cooperate with an investigation into potential risks to US national security.
In its first statement since the scandal broke, the Singapore-headquartered company said on Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with US export control laws “extremely seriously.”

Details about Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (who founded the company, according to CNBC and Bloomberg) and suspected Chinese spy, are still unclear. Revelations about an alleged second affair, with an Nvidia executive, prompted Nvidia’s board to hold a meeting last night to discuss Huang’s future.
The statement, signed by Megaspeed’s chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan, said:
double quotation markMegaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government.
Nvidia has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.

Megaspeed is a cloud computing firm that operates datacentres across southeast Asia, and is facing renewed scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated the flow of restricted Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars into China.
Several investment banks have downgraded their target price estimates for Nvidia shares.
Analysts at Citi cut their target price again, to $225 from $285.
JPMorgan cut its target price $215 from $320, while Cantor Fitzgerald went down to $250 from $350, and Stifel cut its estimate to $205 from £315.
Melius Research went even further. It switched to a hold rating on the stock, and cut its target price to $185 from $315.
Nvidia shares are trading 7.9% lower at $173.73 in pre-market trading at present.
“If Jensen Huang is forced out, I would expect Nvidia shares to underperform for a period,” said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.

double quotation markNvidia was already facing an unusually demanding expectations bar. The stock was not expensive, but its earnings outlook depended on confidence in exceptional growth and near-flawless execution across the entire AI ecosystem. Jensen has set a very ambitious framework, including roughly 70% year-on-year growth next year. A new CEO will likely want to establish credibility by setting a more conservative bar. The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap, that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system spanning employees, foundry and packaging partners, memory suppliers, systems companies, cloud customers and the financing mechanisms supporting AI deployment. In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself. I would also watch the financing architecture behind AI demand: leasing, customer financing and Nvidia’s investments across the ecosystem. Those arrangements are increasingly important in translating demand into deployed capacity and reported revenue. So, this is not principally a valuation problem, it is a confidence problem. The long-term AI story remains intact: Nvidia still has the industry’s most powerful integrated stack across compute, networking and software, and the valuation offers some support. But the stock could move from a Jensen premium to an execution discount until new leadership proves it can deliver.
In pre-market trading, US chipmakers Intel, Marvell Technology and Micron are down between 1.8% and 2.7%, while AI infrastructure company CoreWeave slid 5.7%.
The declines, if maintained when Wall Street opens, would wipe out Wednesday’s gains, when strong results from CoreWeave, an American specialised GPU cloud-computing provider, lifted AI stocks.

Nebius reversed earlier losses to trade 1% higher, following Wednesday’s 15% jump. The Amsterdam-based, Nasdaq-listed company today beat ⁠Wall Street estimates for third-quarter revenue and projected $12bn to $13bn in sales for 2027, powered ⁠by booming demand ⁠for its cloud computing infrastructure.

AI stocks have seen wild swings, also because the Democrats’ victory in midterm elections intensified concerns about a slowdown in datacentre development that could lead to a wider economic slowdown – while some investors see the pullback as a buying opportunity. Seven in 10 Americans are opposed to the construction of new datacentres for artificial intelligence in their local area. Some Republicans have also endorsed a moratorium on new datacentres, which consume vast amounts of energy and water and lead to pollution.

Last night, we reported that Nvidia appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.
A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation.

Global markets are struggling to maintain yesterday’s attempted recovery, with renewed uncertainty surrounding Nvidia weighing on sentiment towards technology stocks, said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at capital.com.

double quotation markWall Street enjoyed a strong session on Wednesday supported by improving confidence in AI demand. However, US futures have turned lower this morning, with Nasdaq futures particularly vulnerable as investors reassess the risks surrounding one of the most influential companies in the AI investment cycle.
Asian markets were also down, highlighting how fragile the recovery remains despite encouraging signs of demand for AI infrastructure.

The biggest development is the escalation of the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Reports that Nvidia’s board is considering his future at a board meeting last night have transformed what initially appeared to be a reputational issue into a significant leadership risk. Nvidia shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, raising concerns about the potential disruption to the company’s strategy.

double quotation markHuang has been central to Nvidia’s growth and its relationships with major AI customers, meaning an unexpected leadership change could create uncertainty at an already sensitive moment for the sector. However, no departure has been confirmed, and Nvidia’s board has previously stated that it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised. The wider concern is that Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty could undermine confidence in the AI trade just as investors were beginning to regain some optimism about its fundamentals. Recent developments at CoreWeave and strong demand surrounding Anthropic’s potential IPO suggest appetite for AI investment remains substantial. However, the controversy raises questions about governance, succession planning and potentially US-China technology relations. If the investigation uncovers evidence of compromised intellectual property, the consequences could extend beyond Nvidia to semiconductor manufacturers and cloud infrastructure providers. For now, this remains a potential risk rather than an established outcome. With Nvidia’s earnings approaching on 17 November, investors face the unusual challenge of assessing strong underlying demand alongside uncertainty over the company’s leadership.
US stock futures are down, pointing to a lower open on Wall Street later.
The S&P 500 is seen opening 0.4% lower while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is set to fell 0.85%, and Dow futures are flat.

Nvidia shares are now down about 7% in Frankfurt. About $600bn have been wiped off the US chipmaker’s market value since the board announced an investigation into longtime boss Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. On Sunday, he admitted to cheating on his wife with the mysterious Shanghai executive.
Under the company’s bylaws, Jensen Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

Meanwhile, the US news website Axios is reporting that Donald Trump on Thursday authorised a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — and he even consulted Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.
But one administration official repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, Axios reported.
The Nvidia board met last night after the second revelation about Jensen Huang.

In a sharp shift from Sunday when it expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, the board met to discuss his future after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee called Kimberly Powell.
She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.
Farewell Jensen, said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.

double quotation markOne of the most impressive careers is set to end. Huang might have been able somehow to cling on at Nvidia after one revelation (though news about chip shipments made that doubtful), but after two, one of which involving a direct report, his fate is sealed. Nvidia’s shares are moving rapidly to price in a post-Jensen world, and this is weighing on tech stocks globally. Nvidia is much bigger than one man now, but this isn’t the way anyone thought it would happen, and denies the company the chance to set up an orderly transition. The question is now whether this news torpedoes the renewed tech rally.
Germany’s Dax also reached a new all-time high, climbing more than 1% in early trading.
The Frankfurt exchange surged 283 points to 26,944, up 1.06%.
